summary: Skywatchers across the Arctic and Spain observed a total solar eclipse, marking one of the day’s most prominent global space developments. In commercial spaceflight, Virgin Galactic announced it is delaying its resumption of commercial flights until 2027, while Paragon Space Development Corporation laid off personnel following the cancellation of NASA's Gateway lunar space station, whose technology will instead be redirected to build the Artemis moon base. Commercial satellite operations saw Astranis unveil "Perceptor," a geostationary surveillance satellite for space domain awareness, and CesiumAstro acquired a semiconductor specialist to support its constellation expansion. On the defense front, the U.S. Space Force awarded $60 million to five companies for multi-vendor satellite network testing, contracted Impulse Space for two additional maneuvering demonstration vehicles, and awarded Space Kinetic $50 million for space maneuverability efforts. Concurrently, U.S. Space Command expanded its Alabama footprint while outlining strategic capability needs to counter adversary satellite surveillance. In civil space news, NASA astronaut Mike Fincke retired following a 30-year career featuring four spaceflights. Scientific studies revealed that a radiation-shielding vest tested during the Artemis I mission effectively reduces astronaut radiation exposure during solar storms, while separate laboratory research confirmed space travel does not diminish heart muscle cell strength. Additionally, astronomers using NASA’s TESS observatory discovered a rare brown dwarf orbiting a massive, aging star. Looking ahead, industry observers should monitor the U.S. Space Force as it prepares to conduct a live-fly advanced maneuver exercise alongside two planned tactically responsive maneuver test missions.
